The contesting defendants, on the other hand, claim that the suit jote was sold in auction in Title Execution Case No. 525 of 1928 and purchased by one Rajmohan who dedicated the suit land to a deity on 20 April 1944, but Rajmohan who happened to be the shebayet of the deity subsequently transferred the same to the defendants by means of several registered Kabalas of the year 1978. They further plead that the suit was bad for defect of party and also non inclusion of all joint properties. 

 5. Mr. SR Paul, learned Counsel for the petitioners, first argues that the High Court Division was wrong in disposing of the revision case on merit in the absence of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. He next argues that the suit is bad in law for non-joinder of party and also for not bringing into hotch potch all the joint properties. 

 Secondly, no suit can fail by reason merely of non-joinder of parties. Order 1, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes this legal position clear. Thirdly, the general rule that all the joint properties should be included in a suit for partition is not an inflexible one. It can be relaxed and a partial partition allowed, where it is not proved that the parties will be prejudiced or inconvenienced by such partition.
